case: Triassic pseudosuchian from Austria; measurements and comparisons with relatives
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (interactive session, 2026-11-01)

facts.statement: Carinthiasuchus is a new genus whose type species is C. kandutschi.
facts.quote: The type species is C. kandutschi.
is an extinct genus of poposauroid pseudosuchian

facts.statement: It comes from the Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria, dated from the Ladinian to the early Carnian.
facts.quote: from the Ladinian to Early Carnian Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria

facts.statement: It is known from one limestone slab with parts of the skull, a set of tail vertebrae and a section of the tail still articulated.
facts.quote: a slab of limestone containing parts of the skull, a collection of caudal vertebrae, and a more distal part of the tail still preserved in articulation

facts.statement: Georg Kandutsch found it near the village of Jadersdorf in the Gailtal Alps of southern Austria.
facts.quote: The specimen was discovered by Georg Kandutsch near the village of Jadersdorf in the Gailtal Alps of Carinthia in southern Austria.

facts.statement: Its genus name combines the Latin name of Carinthia with the Greek word soúkhos, roughly meaning crocodile.
facts.quote: the Greek soúkhos (σούχος), which roughly translates to crocodile

facts.statement: The species name honours its discoverer, Georg Kandutsch.
facts.quote: The specific name meanwhile was chosen in honor of the animal's discoverer, Georg Kandutsch.

facts.statement: The preserved part of the skull measures about 53 mm, and the complete skull was perhaps up to 65 mm long.
facts.quote: The preserved portion measures approximately 53 mm, which Dalla Vecchia and Cau use as the basis for an estimated total length of perhaps up to 65 mm

facts.statement: Unfused bones show that the individual had not reached full maturity.
facts.quote: indicating that the individual was not yet fully mature

facts.statement: Its skull was far smaller than those of Ticinosuchus and Batrachotomus, which measured 260 mm and up to 500 mm.
facts.quote: Ticinosuchus and Batrachotomus with skull lengths of 260 mm and up to 500 mm respectively

facts.statement: Unlike more derived poposauroids, it kept bony plates (osteoderms) along its tail.
facts.quote: Carinthiasuchus still preserves a distinct series of bony plates running down its tail

facts.statement: The tail osteoderms sit in pairs forming a double row, which becomes a single row towards the tip.
facts.quote: the osteoderms are reduced to a single row

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses make it an early poposauroid close to Qianosuchus from China, though with weak support.
facts.quote: clading closely with Qianosuchus from the Anisian of China, though support for this relationship is low

facts.statement: It can be ruled out from the sail-backed ctenosauriscids and the two-legged shuvosaurids.
facts.quote: Carinthiasuchus can however be confidently excluded from certain derived poposauroid clades such as the sail-backed ctenosauriscids and bipedal shuvosaurids.

facts.statement: Dalla Vecchia and Cau named it in 2026 in the Rivista Italiana di Paleontologia e Stratigrafia.
facts.quote:
Year: 2026
Authors: FABIO MARCO DALLA VECCHIA, ANDREA CAU

sentences.text: Carinthiasuchus was a small poposauroid pseudosuchian whose preserved skull measures about 53 mm, with an estimated complete length of up to 65 mm.

The specimen belonged to an individual that had not finished growing, yet its skull was far smaller than those of relatives such as Ticinosuchus and Batrachotomus, which reached 260 mm and up to 500 mm.
Unlike more advanced poposauroids, it kept bony plates called osteoderms along the tail, arranged in a double row that narrows to a single row near the tip.
Georg Kandutsch discovered the fossil near Jadersdorf, in the Gailtal Alps of southern Austria.
It is a single limestone slab holding pieces of the skull, tail vertebrae and an articulated stretch of the tail.
Its genus name joins Carinthia with the Greek word for crocodile, and the species name honours its discoverer.
Dalla Vecchia and Cau named it in 2026 in the Rivista Italiana di Paleontologia e Stratigrafia.
Their analyses place it near the base of the poposauroids, close to Qianosuchus from China, although this link is weakly supported.
It clearly did not belong to the sail-backed ctenosauriscids or the two-legged shuvosaurids.
It lived between the Ladinian and the early Carnian, in what is now the Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria.
Carinthiasuchus fue un pequeño pseudosuquio poposauroideo cuyo cráneo conservado mide unos 53 mm, con una longitud completa estimada de hasta 65 mm.
El ejemplar pertenecía a un individuo que aún no había terminado de crecer, pero su cráneo era mucho menor que el de parientes como Ticinosuchus y Batrachotomus, que alcanzaban 260 mm y hasta 500 mm.
A diferencia de los poposauroideos más avanzados, conservaba placas óseas llamadas osteodermos a lo largo de la cola, dispuestas en una doble hilera que se reduce a una sola cerca de la punta.
Georg Kandutsch descubrió el fósil cerca de Jadersdorf, en los Alpes del Gailtal, en el sur de Austria.
Se trata de una única losa de caliza con fragmentos del cráneo, vértebras de la cola y un tramo de cola aún articulado.
Su nombre de género une Carintia con la palabra griega para cocodrilo, y el de la especie homenajea a su descubridor.
Dalla Vecchia y Cau le dieron nombre en 2026 en la Rivista Italiana di Paleontologia e Stratigrafia.
Sus análisis lo sitúan cerca de la base de los poposauroideos, próximo a Qianosuchus de China, aunque este parentesco tiene poco apoyo.
Sin duda no pertenecía a los ctenosaurísquidos con vela ni a los shuvosáuridos bípedos.
Vivió entre el Ladiniense y el Carniense inicial, en lo que hoy es la Formación Partnach de Carintia, en Austria.
